h1:
First Time in Roi Et
What to Know + 2-Day Plan
intro: Roi Et is an easygoing Isan town — small enough that the whole center is walkable. You get a 35-storey observation tower, a lake park right downtown, pretty temples, and the famous Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice grown nearby. If it's your first time and you're not sure where to start, this guide covers it all: getting there, where to stay, what to eat, and a 2-day, 1-night itinerary that actually flows.

blocks.html: Roi Et sits in the middle of Isan, and plenty of people drive straight through it on the way to Khon Kaen or Mukdahan without stopping. The town is more worth a visit than you'd think. The headliners are Roi Et Tower, an observation tower with one of Thailand's first glass-floor skywalks, and Bueng Phlan Chai, the downtown lake park where locals actually come out to live their evenings. Two days is plenty to see it all on a first visit — no need to rush.

blocks.text: Where Roi Et is and how to get there

blocks.html: Roi Et is in central Isan, about 500 km from Bangkok and only an hour and a half from Khon Kaen — which is why a lot of people fly into Khon Kaen and drive over. If you'd rather head straight into town, Roi Et has its own airport.

items: By plane — Roi Et Airport has flights from Don Mueang, about an hour in the air. The airport is around 13 km from town; grab a taxi or rental car from there.

By bus — From Bangkok's Mo Chit terminal to Roi Et bus station takes about 6–7 hours, with fares around 450–630 THB. There are daytime departures and overnight sleeper coaches. Operators on this route include Nakhonchai Air, Transport Co. (999), and several private companies.

Connecting from Khon Kaen — If you fly into Khon Kaen, vans to Roi Et run very frequently, leaving roughly every hour from morning till evening. The ride is about an hour and a half — handy if you can find cheaper flights into Khon Kaen.
Driving yourself — Easiest if you want to get out to Thung Kula Ronghai or Ku Ka Sing outside town, since public transport doesn't reach those spots.

blocks.title: Which to pick
blocks.html: If you're only doing the town itself, you don't need a car — motorcycle taxis or ride-hailing apps will do. But if you plan to head out to the jasmine rice fields or the stone sanctuary, renting a car or driving yourself is a lot smoother.

blocks.text: Where to stay and which area is handiest

blocks.html: Roi Et's center is small, so staying around Bueng Phlan Chai or near Roi Et Tower is the most convenient — you can walk to the main landmarks, and in the evening there are restaurants and markets to wander. Hotels in town range from local spots in the high-hundreds of baht up to mid-range places with a pool.

items: Around Bueng Phlan Chai — Right downtown, great for evening strolls, close to food and restaurants. Ideal if you don't have a car.
Near Roi Et Tower — A bit quieter, but only a few minutes by car or motorcycle taxi into the center.
Along the bypass road — Newer hotels with plenty of parking. Good if you've driven in and aren't fussed about walking to sights.

items.name: Roi Et Tower
items.blurb: A 35-storey observation tower with 360-degree views over Roi Et and a glass-floor skywalk. Entry is around 50 THB, and the top floor has the city's principal Buddha image to pay respects to.

items.name: Bueng Phlan Chai
items.blurb: A free downtown lake park with an island in the middle, the city pillar shrine, and fish to feed. In the evening locals come out to exercise and stroll, and it gets lively.

items.name: Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon
items.blurb: A huge white-and-gold pagoda in Nong Phok district, mixing central Thai and Isan architecture. Climb to the upper levels for mountain views. It's about an hour-plus outside town.

blocks.html: With more time, head over to Wat Burapha Phiram, home to a very tall standing Buddha in the blessing pose — a signature photo spot for the city. Or go farther out to Thung Kula Ronghai, the famous GI jasmine rice fields, and Ku Ka Sing, a Khmer-era stone sanctuary in Kaset Wisai district.

blocks.text: What to eat when you're in Roi Et

blocks.html: Roi Et is true Isan, so the food leans bold and spicy — som tam, larb, koi, and grilled chicken are easy to find on every corner. The one thing worth going out of your way for is rice cooked from Thung Kula jasmine rice, plus the local spots where townsfolk actually eat.

items.name: Khanom Jeen Baan Khun Ya
items.blurb: A popular khanom jeen (rice noodle) spot in town with around 9 curry sauces to choose from, soft noodles, and fresh veggies on the side. On weekends there's live music at lunchtime.

items.name: Tom Kai Baan 3 Phi Nong
items.blurb: A homey, wallet-friendly restaurant known for boiled and fried free-range chicken, big-tray som tam, and a range of Isan dishes. Locals bring the whole family here.

items.name: Isan Liap Pak Kon
items.blurb: Bold Isan and seafood dishes. The most-ordered items are barbecue pork ribs and salt-grilled prawns. Open from evening till late, good for a long, lingering dinner.

items.name: Bangkok 33
items.blurb: A chill spot with several zones and a menu mixing Thai and Western — German pork knuckle, grilled river prawns, salmon steak. Open till midnight, good for groups or a special meal.

items.name: Evening market around Bueng Phlan Chai
items.blurb: Lakeside evening snacks — grilled bites, som tam, desserts. Eat as you walk and take in the lake views. This is what an Isan dinner looks like for Roi Et locals.

blocks.title: The souvenir to buy
blocks.html: Before you head home, pick up some Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice — Roi Et's GI-certified rice makes a great gift, fragrant and high quality. You'll find it at souvenir shops around town and at rice co-op stores.
This plan is built for first-timers staying in town. It works through the in-town landmarks first, then moves out of town on day two. Adjust the timings however you like — no rush.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Around town: temples and tower views

items.activity: Start at Wat Burapha Phiram to pay respects at the tall standing Buddha and grab a photo of the city's signature image.
Head up Roi Et Tower for 360-degree views over the city and a walk across the glass-floor skywalk.
items.note: Entry around 50 THB; clear days let you see far.

items.activity: Lunch at Khanom Jeen Baan Khun Ya or Tom Kai Baan 3 Phi Nong.
items.note: Popular spots — they get busy at lunch.

items.activity: Rest at the hotel to dodge the afternoon heat, or find a café in town to chill.
items.note: Isan afternoons are hot — take a break first.

items.activity: Stroll around Bueng Phlan Chai, feed the fish, watch locals work out.
items.note: Free entry; evening is the best time.

items.activity: Dinner at the lakeside market or Isan Liap Pak Kon.
items.note: Graze the lakeside snacks at your own pace.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Out of town: the great pagoda and jasmine rice fields

items.activity: Set off for Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon in Nong Phok district.
items.note: About an hour-plus drive; leave early to beat the midday heat.

items.activity: Visit Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon, climb to the upper levels for mountain views and to pay respects.
Find a local restaurant around Nong Phok for lunch.
items.note: Ask the village eateries nearby — prices are easy.

items.activity: Stop at Thung Kula Ronghai to see the jasmine rice fields and buy rice as a souvenir.
items.note: Green or golden paddy season looks best.

items.activity: Head back into town, pack up, and grab souvenirs before you leave.
items.note: Leave buffer time if you need to return a rental car or catch an evening bus.

blocks.html: If you've only got one day, drop day two and just do the town — you'll still get the full picture of Roi Et. With 3 days, add Ku Ka Sing, the Khmer stone sanctuary, or carry on to nearby Khon Kaen and Maha Sarakham.

blocks.text: Small things worth knowing before you go

items: When to go — The best weather is late rainy season into early cool season, roughly November to February. Isan summers are scorching, so avoid outdoor sightseeing around midday.
Getting around town — There's no real city bus network. Motorcycle taxis, ride-hailing apps, or a rented motorbike are the smoothest options.
Cash — Local shops and markets often take cash or scan-to-pay; keep some cash on you for the smaller places.
Bun Phawet festival — Come in March and you might catch Bun Phawet, the town's well-known traditional festival. Rooms fill up fast, so book ahead.

blocks.title: The first-timer takeaway
blocks.html: For a first visit to Roi Et, plan 2 days and 1 night, stay in town, do Roi Et Tower–Bueng Phlan Chai–temples on day one, then head out of town on day two. Eat real Isan food, buy jasmine rice to take home, and you'll have a full sense of the place.

faq.q: How many days do I need for a first trip to Roi Et?
faq.a: Two days and one night is just right for a first-timer. Day one covers the town — Roi Et Tower, Bueng Phlan Chai, and the temples. Day two heads out of town to Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon and Thung Kula Ronghai. If you only have one day, just doing the town still gives you the full picture.

faq.q: Can I visit Roi Et without my own car?
faq.a: The town itself is easy — use motorcycle taxis or a ride-hailing app, since the in-town landmarks are close together. But to get out to Thung Kula Ronghai or Ku Ka Sing outside town, renting or chartering a car is recommended, as public transport doesn't reach them.

faq.q: What's the best way to get from Bangkok to Roi Et?
faq.a: Take a coach from Mo Chit, about 6–7 hours, with fares around 450–630 THB. Or fly into Roi Et Airport from Don Mueang and take a car into town. Another option is to fly into Khon Kaen and connect to Roi Et by road, about another hour and a half.

faq.q: What food is Roi Et known for?
faq.a: It's true Isan, so the food is bold and spicy — som tam, larb, koi, grilled chicken. Well-known spots in town include Khanom Jeen Baan Khun Ya and Tom Kai Baan 3 Phi Nong. The must-buy souvenir is GI-certified Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice.

faq.q: When should I visit Roi Et?
faq.a: The best weather is late rainy season into early cool season, roughly November to February, when outdoor sightseeing is comfortable. If you want a traditional festival, March brings Bun Phawet, the town's big event — but rooms fill up fast, so book ahead.
